content_html:
Web Developer Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A web developer resume has to prove one thing above all: that you can ship working sites. Hiring managers do not hire on a list of languages. They hire on live work — sites that load fast, work on every screen, and stay up — and they check all three before they ever call you.

This guide gives you a full annotated example, the skills hiring sides actually scan for, and the mistakes that quietly cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works: what you built, who used it, and what changed.

Quick answer: A web developer resume should lead with live project links and your core stack — HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and your framework; name the sites or apps you shipped and the result of each; list the tools hiring teams scan for; and keep the layout single-column with standard headings so tracking systems parse every section cleanly.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with shipped work — live links, your stack, and the result of each project.
  • Prove impact with before-and-after numbers: load times, conversions, and users reached.
  • Name the exact stack and tools from the posting: framework, language, testing, and deployment.
  • Every bullet pairs a task with a result: what you built, who used it, and what changed.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Web Development Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to an engineering manager or a tech lead and you will not hear "passionate about code." You will hear:

  • Live work first. Links to shipped sites beat adjectives — a portfolio with three working sites tells a hiring manager more than a page of framework names.
  • Speed and reliability. Load times, uptime, and bug counts are what developers are judged on. "Cut page load from 3.2 seconds to 0.9 seconds" is a hiring signal; "responsible for website performance" is not.
  • Range across the stack. Front-end depth plus enough back-end and deployment knowledge to ship without hand-holding — name the framework, the language, and the tools you used in production.
  • Team habits. Code review, Git workflow, testing, and documentation — hiring managers want work that survives the next person who touches it.
  • Accessibility and responsive design. Sites that work for every visitor on every screen — if your work only looks right on your own laptop, it is not finished.

If your resume reads like a course list — all frameworks, no shipped work — it will lose to a release log.

Web Developer Resume Example

Below is a complete example for a front-end developer with agency experience. It is fictional — the name and figures are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern hiring managers respond to: what you built, who used it, and what changed.

ALEX RIVERA — Front-End Web Developer
Austin, TX · (512) 555-0147 · alex.rivera@email.com · alexrivera.dev · github.com/alexrivera-dev

SUMMARY
Front-end web developer with 4 years shipping responsive sites for e-commerce and SaaS clients. Rebuilt a checkout flow that cut page load from 3.2 seconds to 0.9 seconds and lifted completed purchases by 22%; shipped 12 client sites and keep 8 production sites at 99.9% uptime. React, TypeScript, and Next.js daily; accessibility-first.

SKILLS
HTML5 · CSS3 · JavaScript (ES2022) · TypeScript · React · Next.js · Vue · Tailwind CSS · Node.js · REST APIs · Git · GitHub Actions · Jest · Cypress · Figma · Vite · Webpack · Responsive design · Accessibility (WCAG) · Core Web Vitals · Docker · AWS Amplify

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Front-End Web Developer — BrightCart Commerce, Austin, TX | 2023–Present - Rebuilt the checkout flow in React and Next.js, cutting page load from 3.2 seconds to 0.9 seconds and lifting completed purchases by 22% in the first quarter - Built a library of 40+ reusable React components that cut new landing-page build time from 3 days to 4 hours - Led an accessibility remediation across 60+ pages, lifting the Lighthouse accessibility score from 71 to 98 with no regressions in the next two releases - Wrote a Cypress test suite covering 120+ user flows that cut production bugs by 35% in six months - Mentor 2 junior developers on code review, Git workflow, and component design; both now ship independently

Web Developer — NorthLoop Digital Agency, Austin, TX | 2021–2023 - Shipped 12 client websites — e-commerce stores, restaurant sites, a nonprofit donation platform — from brief to launch - Built headless CMS sites with Next.js and a content API, letting clients publish new pages without developer help - Improved the agency's average client PageSpeed score from 58 to 91 across 10 sites in one year - Maintained 8 production sites at 99.9% uptime, including weekend deploys and incident response - Ran handover training for 5 clients, cutting post-launch support tickets by a third

Freelance Web Developer | 2020–2021 - Built 6 small-business websites with booking, menus, and contact forms — all responsive, all delivered on schedule - Set up analytics and search basics for each client so owners could see visits and enquiries unaided

EDUCATION
B.S., Computer Science — University of Texas at Austin, 2020 Full-Stack Web Development Certificate — freeCodeCamp, 2020

Why it works: the summary leads with the two things engineering managers check first — a live result (checkout load from 3.2 seconds to 0.9 seconds) and shipped volume (12 client sites) — then names the stack. Every bullet pairs a build with a result: faster pages, fewer bugs, clients who can publish alone.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: shipped work, stack, result

"Cut page load from 3.2 seconds to 0.9 seconds," "12 client sites," "React, TypeScript, Next.js" — three facts that let an engineering manager place you in thirty seconds. Lead with shipped work and a result, not with your training.

Experience: builds with outcomes, not duties

Each bullet should answer "what changed because you built it?" "Built websites for clients" is a duty; "lifted completed purchases by 22% by rebuilding the checkout flow" is proof. Load time, conversion, uptime, bug counts, and pages shipped are the metrics developers are judged on — put at least three on your resume.

Portfolio: links a hiring manager can click

Your portfolio is the closest thing to proof a developer gets. Link the live site, not a screenshot, and add the GitHub repository where the code is public. One broken link costs more than a missing skill — check every link the week you apply, and keep the portfolio fast and responsive, because it is being judged as your work.

Skills: mirror the posting, honestly

List the stack you have actually shipped with, in the posting's own words — "React" versus "React.js" matters to filters, and so does "TypeScript" versus "JavaScript." Do not list a framework you only followed in a tutorial; the technical screen will find it out. Depth in one stack beats a long list of half-known tools.

Web Developer Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting's language exactly — "Next.js" vs "React" matters to filters:

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES2022), TypeScript, SQL, Python
  • Frameworks & libraries: React, Next.js, Vue, Tailwind CSS, Node.js, Express
  • Quality & performance: responsive design, accessibility (WCAG), Core Web Vitals, Lighthouse, Jest, Cypress, cross-browser testing
  • Tools & process: Git, GitHub Actions, Figma, Vite, Webpack, Docker, REST APIs, CI/CD, Agile

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Agencies and product teams screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. 5 Mistakes That Cost Web Developers Interviews

  1. Dead portfolio links. A link to a site that is down, or a repository that is private, reads as no portfolio at all. Check every link the week you apply.
  2. Listing every framework you ever touched. A long stack list with no depth fails the first technical screen. List what you have shipped with.
  3. Duties without results. "Built websites for clients" could describe any developer. Add the result — faster load, more purchases, fewer bugs — to every bullet.
  4. Hiding the portfolio. If your best work sits at the bottom of page two, it may never reach a human. Put live links in the header or summary.
  5. Ignoring accessibility and mobile. A site that only works on a desktop, or that screen readers cannot use, tells a hiring manager your work is unfinished. Test on a phone and a keyboard before you call a project done.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a degree to become a web developer?

No. Most employers hire on proof of skill — a portfolio of shipped sites, a GitHub profile with real commits, and the ability to pass a technical screen — rather than a degree. Bootcamps, self-study, and freelance work all count when the work is live and the code is yours.

Do web developers need a portfolio?

Yes — a portfolio is the closest thing to proof a developer gets. Three live sites with clean code behind them carry more weight than any skills list. If you have no client work yet, build two or three complete projects of your own and deploy them.

What if I have no professional experience?

Lead with projects. A deployed site with real users, an open-source contribution, or a freelance build all count as shipped work. Name what you built, who used it, and what changed — the same pattern as any job bullet.

Should I list every framework I have touched?

No. List the stack you have actually shipped with, in the posting's own words. A short honest list beats a long one that falls apart under questions.

How long should a web developer resume be?

One page for most developers, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a long career across genuinely different work — agency, product, and freelance — and even then keep your portfolio links and best result on page one.

Can web developers work remotely?

Yes — remote development is one of the most common remote roles in tech. Remote postings still check the same things: shipped work, speed, reliability, and a track record of working without on-site supervision, plus clear written communication in code reviews and stand-ups.
